courses.title: Introduction to Biomedical Engineering and Circuits
courses.description: Scope of biomedical engineering, electrical circuit fundamentals, electrical safety in hospitals, and an introduction to medical devices and their regulation.

topics.title: Scope of Biomedical Engineering
topics.summary: What biomedical engineers do, subfields and the role of clinical engineering in hospitals.

material.heading: Subfields
material.body: Biomedical engineering applies engineering principles to medicine and biology. Subfields include bioinstrumentation (designing devices that measure physiological signals, e.g. ECG machines, pulse oximeters), biomechanics (forces in the body, implants, prosthetics), biomaterials (materials compatible with body tissues), medical imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound), rehabilitation engineering (assistive devices), tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, biosignal processing, and clinical engineering (management and maintenance of medical equipment in hospitals).

material.heading: Clinical engineering in Nigeria
material.body: A large share of medical equipment in low- and middle-income countries is estimated to be out of service, often because of lack of maintenance, spare parts, training or suitable power supply. Clinical engineers plan procurement, commission and inventory equipment, schedule preventive maintenance, perform safety testing and train users. Appropriate technology — robust, affordable, repairable devices that work with unstable electricity (e.g. solar-powered oxygen concentrators and vaccine refrigerators) — is especially important in Nigeria.
keyPoints: Much equipment is out of service in LMICs

topics.title: DC Circuit Fundamentals
topics.summary: Charge, current, voltage, resistance, Kirchhoff's laws and power.

material.heading: Basic quantities
material.body: Electric current is the flow of charge (I = Q/t, amperes). Voltage (potential difference) is energy per unit charge (volts). Resistance opposes current (ohms); Ohm's law: V = IR. Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R (watts). Series resistors add (R = R1 + R2); parallel resistors combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. A voltage divider gives Vout = Vin × R2/(R1 + R2), used in sensor circuits.
keyPoints: Voltage divider: Vout = Vin × R2/(R1 + R2)

material.heading: Kirchhoff's laws, capacitors and inductors
material.body: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving (conservation of charge). Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero (conservation of energy). A capacitor stores charge (Q = CV; unit farad) and blocks DC while passing AC; an RC circuit charges with time constant τ = RC (reaching ~63% in one τ). Defibrillators store energy in capacitors (E = ½CV²). An inductor opposes changes in current (unit henry).
keyPoints: KCL: currents at a node sum to zero
KVL: voltages around a loop sum to zero

topics.title: AC Circuits and Power Supplies
topics.summary: Alternating current, RMS values, impedance, transformers, rectifiers and power quality.

material.heading: Alternating current
material.body: Mains electricity in Nigeria is AC at 230 V (nominal; historically 220–240 V), 50 Hz. For a sinusoid, Vrms = Vpeak/√2 (so 230 V rms ≈ 325 V peak). Capacitive reactance Xc = 1/(2πfC) falls with frequency; inductive reactance XL = 2πfL rises with frequency. Impedance (Z) combines resistance and reactance. Filters exploit reactance: low-pass filters remove high-frequency noise; high-pass filters remove baseline drift; a notch filter at 50 Hz removes mains interference from ECG signals.
keyPoints: 50 Hz notch filter for ECG interference

material.heading: Power supplies and power quality
material.body: Transformers step voltage up or down (Vs/Vp = Ns/Np) and can provide isolation. Diodes allow current in one direction; rectifiers convert AC to DC, smoothed by capacitors and stabilised by voltage regulators. Unstable grid supply, surges and generator switching damage equipment; protective measures include automatic voltage regulators/stabilisers, surge protectors and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) for critical devices such as ventilators, incubators and laboratory analysers. Solar photovoltaic systems with batteries and inverters are increasingly used in health facilities.
keyPoints: UPS and stabilisers protect critical equipment

topics.title: Electrical Safety in Health Care
topics.summary: Physiological effects of current, macroshock and microshock, earthing and equipment classes.

material.heading: Effects of current
material.body: The effect of electric current on the body depends on magnitude, pathway, duration and frequency. At 50/60 Hz through the trunk: about 1 mA is the threshold of perception; 10–20 mA causes 'let-go' failure (sustained muscle contraction); about 100 mA can cause ventricular fibrillation (macroshock). Microshock occurs when current is applied directly to the heart (e.g. via pacing wires or catheters): as little as 10–100 µA can cause fibrillation, so leakage currents in cardiac-connected equipment must be tiny. Low-frequency AC (50 Hz) is more dangerous than DC or high-frequency currents (which is why electrosurgery at >300 kHz does not stimulate nerves).
keyPoints: 1 mA: perception; 10–20 mA: can't let go; ~100 mA: VF
Microshock: µA directly to the heart

material.heading: Protection
material.body: Protective measures include protective earthing (grounding), fuses and circuit breakers, residual current devices (RCD/earth-leakage breakers that trip at about 30 mA imbalance), double insulation and isolated power supplies. IEC 60601 classifies equipment: Class I (protective earth), Class II (double insulation, no earth) and internally powered; applied parts are Type B, BF (floating) and CF (cardiac floating — lowest leakage, for direct cardiac connection). Routine electrical safety testing checks earth continuity, insulation resistance and leakage current.
keyPoints: Type CF applied parts for direct cardiac use

topics.title: Medical Devices: Classification and Regulation
topics.summary: Risk classes, device lifecycle, and regulation of medical devices in Nigeria.

material.heading: Classification
material.body: Medical devices are classified by risk, e.g. in the EU/Global Harmonization approach: Class I (low risk — bandages, stethoscopes, tongue depressors), Class IIa (low–moderate — hearing aids, ultrasound scanners), Class IIb (moderate–high — ventilators, infusion pumps, X-ray machines) and Class III (high risk — implantable pacemakers, heart valves, drug-eluting stents). The US FDA uses Classes I, II and III. Higher classes require more rigorous clinical evidence and conformity assessment.
keyPoints: Class I: low risk; Class III: high risk (implants)
Ventilators and infusion pumps: Class IIb

material.heading: Lifecycle and regulation
material.body: The device lifecycle includes needs assessment, design, verification and validation, regulatory approval, procurement, installation and commissioning, user training, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning/disposal. Quality management for manufacturers follows ISO 13485, and risk management follows ISO 14971. In Nigeria, NAFDAC registers medical devices, and the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) sets product standards. Adverse events and device failures should be reported (post-market surveillance/vigilance).

questions.stem: An implantable cardiac pacemaker is a Class ___ device.
questions.explanation: Implantable life-sustaining devices are high-risk Class III.

questions.stem: A stethoscope is an example of a Class ___ device.
questions.explanation: Low-risk, non-invasive devices are Class I.
